newsitem.title: UK: Forty British cancer victims sue two tobacco firms.
newsitem.headline: Forty British cancer victims sue two tobacco firms.

text.p: Forty British cancer sufferers plan to sue two tobacco companies for failing to change their products to limit the dangers of smoking in a case that could open the door to thousands of similar claims, lawyers said on Friday.

The group action against Imperial Tobacco and Gallahers, who have 80 percent of the British cigarette market, will be the first in Britain in which the plantiffs will be represented by lawyers working on a no-win, no-fee basis.
The 40 were refused state funding for the legal costs in July on the grounds that their case was unlikely to succeed.

"Following the decision of the (Legal Aid) Board...it was clear that the only way for the tobacco victims to gain access to justice in the British courts was for lawyers to take on the cases through the no-win, no-fee scheme," lawyer Martyn Day, co-ordinator of the claims, said in a statement on Friday.

The case is based on the alleged failure of the tobacco companies, which produce such brands as Benson and Hedges, Players, Embassy and Silk Cut, to reduce the levels of tar in their cigarettes after doctors in the late 1950s began saying tar could lead to the onset of cancer.
The tobacco companies argue that there is no proof that by reducing the tar levels in cigarettes these people would not have suffered from cancer.

Under the agreement, the lawyers will receive no fee if the cancer victims lose the case but could earn an estimated three million pounds ($4.7 million) in legal fees and a similar amount from the plantiffs if they are successful.
"I was of the view before the Board's decision that the claims are strong. I am still of that view," Day said.
One of the plantiffs, lung cancer victim Anthony Bywater, said he was desperately disappointed when legal aid was denied but felt sure he would win the case.
"It is a risk for all of us in taking on the tobacco companies but I am confident we will end up victorious."
Leigh, Day and Co, the London firm which is handling the case, said it anticipates many other lung cancer victims will join the claim.

"With over 30,000 of them (lung cancer sufferers) dying a year as a result of smoking in the UK, it provides an almost inexhaustible supply of claimants to take on the companies," it said in a statement.
Imperial Tobacco and Gallaher, a unit of American Brands of the United States, were confident of winning the case.

"In the last 40 years, hundreds of such cases have been brought against tobacco companies worldwide and none of them has resulted in any tobacco company paying any damages at all," a spokesman for Imperial Tobacco told BBC radio.
Jeff Jeffery, of Gallaher, said it was the company's policy not to comment on matters pending litigation.
Under the English legal system one judge is likely to be appointed to deal with the tobacco claims which lawyers hope will come to court within the next two years.
ASH, a charity campaigning for the reduction of smoking in Britain, applauded the legal action.
"The tobacco companies had a duty of care to their consumers which they chose to ignore. Now is the time for them to pay the price of their neglect," the group said.

Earlier this year in the United States, where hundreds of suits against the tobacco industry have been filed, Liggett Group became the first tobacco company to agree to settle a class action case in New Orleans and to negotiate with states in their litigation to recoup the health costs of smokers.
